storyline: Every record in the sky is a number, and in astronomy each number has to be earned from the one before it, so this journey climbs one question at a time. It starts with how far, because a distance, caught by parallax, is what turns how bright a star looks into how much light it truly makes. Power raises the next question, whether a star makes its light by being hot or by being big, and color answers the first half. Divide the power by what each square meter of a surface that hot gives out and the size falls out, and the biggest stars turn out to be heavy stars swollen near their ends. Heavy stars die first, so the stars missing from a crowd tell its age, and dating a crowd means knowing exactly how bright each kind of star truly is. The climb ends where it began, at distance, run backward: a star of known power, seen faint, says how far away it is.

beats.label: How much light: the most powerful
How hot: the hottest and coolest
How big: the largest and smallest
How old: the oldest stars and richest crowds
How far, run backward: the farthest

question.A7-record-breakers: How can a point of light tell you a star is the biggest, hottest or oldest?
How do astronomers crown the sky's record holders from nothing but their light?
How far up the sky's record book can plain starlight take you?
hook.A7-record-breakers: Every record in the sky starts with one number: how far away the star is.
Know a star's distance, and its light starts answering questions it used to hide.
The sky's records form a chain, and the first link is always a distance.
story.A7-record-breakers: Each record tonight answers a question the one before it raised and could not settle. Starting with {hook}, a distance turns brightness into power, and every number after that is built from the last.

A record means nothing without a measurement behind it, and tonight the measurements come in the order they depend on one another. Each stop takes what the one before it settled and asks what it left open.
Begin with {hook} and a single distance, and watch that one number unlock the next record and the one after it, until {name} closes the climb.
payoff.A7-record-breakers: From {hook} to {name}, every record was crowned by measurement rather than by looks, and each measurement stood on the one before it. A distance turns brightness into power, power and color give size, and the lifespans of heavy stars date whole crowds. Run the chain backward and stars of known power measure the farthest light, so a few honest numbers, earned in order, reach from the Sun's neighbors to other galaxies.

The night's records ran from {hook} to {name}, and none of them could have been read on its own. Behind every one stands the same short chain: a parallax, then a brightness, then a power, then whatever that power, joined to a color, reveals. That ordinary binoculars reach all of them is a quiet record of its own, the reach of one human eye stretched by a few centuries of careful measuring.

{name} capped a ladder of records that began with {hook}, and every rung was a measurement resting on the one below it. What makes a star a record holder is never how it looks but what the numbers hidden in its light reveal once they are read in the right order. The same ladder keeps climbing, out to galaxies whose distances rest on exactly these steps.
story.A7-record-breakers.end3: Tonight climbs the first rungs of the record book: how far a star is, then how much light it truly makes, then how hot its surface runs. Starting with {hook}, each answer opens the next question, and by {name} a star's color has become a thermometer.

A record means nothing without a measurement behind it, and tonight's records come in the order the measurements depend on one another: how far, how powerful, how hot. By the end, brightness alone will have been unmasked as the poor judge it is.
Begin with {hook} and a distance, turn brightness into power, and then ask how a star makes all that light. {name} closes a short climb in which every rung stands on the one below it.
story.A7-record-breakers.end4: Nobody has ever laid a ruler across a star, yet tonight ends with a star's size, built from nothing but its light. Starting with {hook}, each record hands the next one a number, until {name} turns those numbers into a body.

Tonight's records climb one question at a time, each answer opening the next, until the night ends among the bodies of stars. Their sizes are measured rather than guessed, built from nothing but the light that reaches you.
Begin with {hook} and follow the records upward until {name}, where the question is no longer how far or how bright but how big, and the answer has to come from light alone.
story.A7-record-breakers.end5: Tonight's climb runs from single stars to whole crowds, where the record is written in time. Starting with {hook}, each answer opens the next question, until {name} is dated by the stars it has already lost.

A record means nothing without a measurement behind it, and tonight's measurements climb from single stars to the age of whole crowds. The rule that dates them is the simplest in astronomy: heavy stars burn out first.
Begin with {hook} and a measurement, and each record hands its number to the next, until {name}, where the stars that are missing become a clock.
story.A7-record-breakers.end6: The last record of the night is distance again, the question astronomy answered first, now answered the other way round. Starting with {hook}, each record hands its number up the ladder until {name}, whose distance could only be read once the rungs beneath it held.

A record means nothing without a measurement behind it, and tonight's climb ends with the record that needs the most of them, the farthest light your eyes can catch, measured by running the first rung backward.
Begin with {hook}, climb through what each measurement unlocks, and arrive at {name}, where stars whose true output is already known, seen faint, hand the distance back.
payoff.A7-record-breakers.end3: From {hook} to {name}, every record rested on the one before it: a distance first, then the true power it reveals, and finally a temperature read from color. Brightness alone would have misjudged tonight's stars badly, crowning near, modest stars over distant giants. Put power and temperature together and the next number falls out, a star's size, and from there the same arithmetic climbs to the ages of star cities and the distances of galaxies.

Tonight's ladder had three rungs, a distance, a power and a temperature, and each could only be climbed from the one below. A star's glow mixes how much light it makes with how far that light has traveled, and its color says how much of that light leaves each square meter of its surface. Divide one by the other and you have the size of a star nobody could ever measure with a ruler, the rung that waits just above the three you climbed.

{name} capped a short climb that began with {hook}: first a distance, then a power, then the heat that helps explain it. The most powerful stars often look far less impressive than they are, because their light has the longest road to travel. That gap between looks and truth is the whole reason astronomers measure, and it widens with every rung above this one.
payoff.A7-record-breakers.end4: From {hook} to {name}, every record rested on the measurements below it, and the last of them, the size of a star, needs all of them at once. A star's width comes from how much light it pours out and how hot each patch of its surface glows, and those two numbers in turn need its distance and its color. The largest stars turn out to be heavy ones swollen near the ends of their lives, and because heavy stars die first, the same ladder climbs on from here to the ages of whole crowds of stars.

Tonight's records climbed to a star's body, and the climb was the point: a width cannot be worked out without a distance, a power and a temperature, each of which has to be earned first. Interferometers now check those sizes directly, combining telescopes to see disks a few thousandths of an arcsecond across, and the two methods agree. That agreement is what makes a size record trustworthy, and the same ladder keeps climbing, out to the ages of star cities and the distances of galaxies.

{name} closed a ladder of records that began with {hook}, and the last rung asked the hardest question, how big a star truly is. The answer came from light alone, without anyone ever holding a ruler to a star. Seen this way, the points of light in any sky become bodies, from crushed cores about the size of the Earth to swollen giants wider than the orbit of Mars.
payoff.A7-record-breakers.end5: From {hook} to {name}, every record rested on the measurements below it, and the last turned from light to time. Because heavy stars burn out first, a crowd's age is written in which of its members are already gone. Applied to the oldest clusters in the galaxy, the same rule gives ages within a whisker of the age of the universe itself, a match between starlight and cosmology that no one planned.

Tonight's ladder ended with time, where records are set in years and in numbers of stars rather than in brightness. A crowd is dated by the rule that heavy stars burn out first, so the richest and oldest are measured with the same physics as the single stars before them. The oldest of them formed when the galaxy was young, and their light is the nearest thing to a fossil that binoculars can show.

{name} closed a climb that began with {hook}, and its record is one no single glance can read: an age, counted from the stars that are missing rather than seen in those that remain. Every such number stands on the ones beneath it, the distances that give true power and the colors that give heat and size. Some crowds dated this way were already old when the Sun was born, and their stars are still shining for you tonight.
payoff.A7-record-breakers.end6: From {hook} to {name}, the climb ended with the question astronomy answered first, how far. Parallax settled it for the nearest stars, and everything else followed from there, power, heat, size and age, until each kind of star had a known true brightness. Turned around, that knowledge measures the farthest light, a star of known power seen faint, which is how a smudge in your binoculars came to have a distance at all.

Tonight's ladder ended at its top rung, the farthest light, and that light carries a record of time as well, since it left its source long before most of human history. Measuring that distance took every method below it, each one calibrated on the last, from the yearly shift of nearby stars to the rhythm of pulsing ones. None of tonight's record holders was ranked by its looks, and the farthest of them looks least of all like what it is.

{name} capped a ladder of records that began with {hook}, and its distance is the one that leans on the most rungs at once. A parallax gave the first distances, those gave the true power of stars of every kind, and stars of known power, found far away, gave the rest. The ladder does not stop here, for the same reasoning reaches galaxies so remote that their light set out before the Earth existed.

HR5459.beat: How far: the nearest star you can see
HR5459.question: How do we know Alpha Centauri is the closest star you can see?
HR5459.why: A star's brightness mixes how much light it makes with how far that light has come, so the climb begins by fixing the distance, at the nearest star the eye can find.
HR5459.look: Find the two Pointers beside the Southern Cross and take the one farther from the Cross. Binoculars show a single brilliant yellow-white point, its two Sun-like stars far too close to split, and beside it blue-white Hadar, which looks nearly as bright from roughly eighty times farther away.
HR5459.answer: Its yearly shift puts it about 4.4 light-years away, and Proxima, the system's faint red third star, is closer still, the nearest single star of all. With the distance fixed, the glare becomes a measurement: the brighter of its two suns makes about one and a half times the Sun's light, and any star with a distance can now be asked how much light it truly makes.
HR5459.story: Alpha Centauri's distance can be checked by a second route that needs no yearly shift at all. Its two Sun-like stars circle each other in about a human lifetime, and the orbit's size can be measured twice, once as an angle on the sky and once in kilometers from the Doppler speeds of the stars in their spectra. Only one distance makes the two sizes agree, and it lands on the parallax result, which is how astronomers know the first rung of the ladder is sound.

STAR-Sirius.beat: How far: the brightest star, and why
STAR-Sirius.question: Is the brightest star in the night sky also the most powerful one?
STAR-Sirius.why: Brightness is the record your eye awards for free, and before it can mean anything you need the one number the eye cannot judge, how far away the star is.
STAR-Sirius.look: Follow Orion's Belt down and to the left to the most brilliant star in the sky. Low down it flashes red and green, which is our air at work rather than the star; then glance up at Rigel and Betelgeuse, two far more powerful stars that look fainter.
STAR-Sirius.answer: Sirius lies about 8.6 light-years away, one of the Sun's nearest neighbors, and at that range its glare works out to only about 25 times the Sun's light, a modest output for so dazzling a star. Brightness mostly rewards closeness, so the real powerhouses are stars that look fainter from much farther off, and only their distances can expose them.
STAR-Sirius.story: The brightness record is kept on a scale that runs backward, inherited from Greek astronomers who called the brightest stars first magnitude. Photometers later turned it into arithmetic, five steps for every hundredfold in light, and the scale had to run below zero to fit the brilliant few. Sirius sits lowest of all, nearly twice as bright as Canopus in second place, and the meter that ranks them says nothing at all about why.

DS-61Cyg.beat: How far: the first distance ever measured
DS-61Cyg.question: How far away is the first star whose distance anyone ever measured?
DS-61Cyg.why: No record in the sky means anything until you can say how far away its holder is, and the very first such number was won here, in 1838.
DS-61Cyg.look: About 8° south-east of Deneb, in Cygnus, a faint star splits in 10× binoculars into two matched orange points. Nothing in the view says near, and that is the surprise: this unassuming pair is well over a hundred times closer than Deneb, the bright star nearby.
DS-61Cyg.answer: 61 Cygni lies about 11 light-years away, which makes it one of the nearest stars you can see without optics, and still its light needs more than a decade to arrive. With that one number, how bright a star looks could at last be turned into how much light it truly makes, and every record of power begins with the same conversion.
DS-61Cyg.story: Bessel won a race that astronomers had been losing for centuries: within a couple of years Thomas Henderson announced a parallax for Alpha Centauri and Friedrich Struve one for Vega. The difficulty was the sheer smallness of the shift, which forced them to beat the sag of the telescope, the bending of starlight by the air and the warmth of the instrument itself. Bessel's heliometer, a telescope with its lens sawn in two, let him measure the pair against fainter background stars night after night, and the yearly swing he found has survived every check since.

HR509.beat: How far: the nearest lone Sun-like star
HR509.question: How close is the nearest lone star of the Sun's own kind?
HR509.why: Records need a baseline, and the fairest one is a star like the Sun, so the first distance here is measured on the nearest lone star of that kind.
HR509.look: About fifteen degrees east of Diphda, the brightest star of Cetus, look for a steady pale-yellow point. The Sun moved out to the same distance would look much like this, only a little brighter, a picture worth carrying through the rest of the records.
HR509.answer: τ Ceti lies about 11.9 light-years away, and from there a star a little dimmer than the Sun is a point you could easily walk past. Hold that picture, because with distances known it becomes a scale: a star that looks this bright from a hundred times farther must be making about ten thousand times as much light.
HR509.story: A star's spectrum works like a label: two stars with matching lines, at matching temperatures, give out similar amounts of light. Nearby stars like this one, whose distances come straight from parallax, are how those labels were calibrated, and with that calibration a Sun-like star too far for parallax can be ranged from its faintness alone. The method, known as spectroscopic parallax, was one of the first ways astronomers reached beyond the stars whose shifts they could measure.

HR1084.beat: How far: a near neighbor with a planet
HR1084.question: How close is the nearest star with both a giant planet and a comet belt?
HR1084.why: Nearness is a record that pays off in detail, since the closer a star, the more of it we can study, and this neighbor is close enough for its planet and dust ring to be found.
HR1084.look: From Zaurak (γ Eridani), in Eridanus, move about 7° west-north-west. You pass δ Eridani first, a shade brighter, and ε Eridani is the next star along, about 2½° beyond it. It is a soft yellow-orange point, unremarkable among its neighbors, which is exactly how one of the closest stars to the Sun looks when it is a little smaller and cooler than the Sun.
HR1084.answer: ε Eridani lies about 10.5 light-years away, which makes it one of the nearest stars of any kind you can see without optics. Its distance also gives away how feeble it is, about a third of the Sun's light, and that turning of how bright into how powerful is the step every bigger record needs.
HR1084.story: Nearness turns distance into detail by simple geometry. At this range one Earth-Sun distance spans about a third of an arcsecond, so a belt of icy debris as far out as our own outer solar system opens to roughly forty arcseconds across, wide enough for telescopes working in submillimeter light to photograph it as a ring. Put the same system much farther away and the ring shrinks to a smudge, which is why the closest stars hold most of the records for what we know about other planetary systems.

HR8387.beat: How far: a faint neighbor, a bright stranger
HR8387.question: Why does one of the Sun's closest neighbors look fainter than Alnair?
HR8387.why: Nearness alone does not make a star bright, and this close neighbor, host to a planet photographed by the Webb telescope, shows the gap between the two records.
HR8387.look: Ten degrees from Alnair, the bright blue-white star of Grus, Epsilon Indi is a modest orange point in faint Indus. Keep the two side by side in your mind: the dim orange one is the near neighbor, and the bright blue-white one is the distant powerhouse.
HR8387.answer: Epsilon Indi gives out about a fifth of the Sun's light, so even at about 12 light-years it is a modest point, while Alnair, roughly eight times farther, outshines it by sheer power. Only the two distances could sort these stars out, and once a distance is known, the light of any star can be weighed the same way.
HR8387.story: Pulling the two apart takes one piece of arithmetic. Alnair looks about three magnitudes brighter, which means roughly sixteen times more light reaching you, and by the time its light arrives it has spread over a sphere some seventy times larger in area. Multiply the two and Alnair turns out to make over a thousand times what this neighbor does, a gap the eye alone would never guess.

AST-Hyades.beat: How far: the nearest star cluster
AST-Hyades.question: How far away is the nearest star cluster, and why does that matter?
AST-Hyades.why: A cluster is a family whose members share one distance, so the nearest family of all is where stars of many kinds can be compared side by side at a known range.
AST-Hyades.look: The V of the Bull's face in Taurus is too big for one view, so sweep along each arm. Every family member you pass sits at nearly the same distance, which makes their differences in brightness and color real; Aldebaran, the bright orange star at one tip, lies in front and does not count.
AST-Hyades.answer: The core of the Hyades lies about 150 light-years away, closer than any other true cluster, so its stars spill past the edges of your field. Because every member shares that distance, their differences in brightness are differences in real power, the number every later record rests on: how much light a star truly makes.
AST-Hyades.story: Long before satellites, the Hyades gave up their distance through perspective. The members move through space in parallel, so their paths across the sky seem to converge on one point, the way railway tracks meet at the horizon, and the angle to that point, combined with each star's speed toward us read from its spectrum, turns a drift in arcseconds into a speed in kilometers per second. Set the two side by side and the distance falls out, and for most of the twentieth century this was the rung on which brighter, farther yardsticks were calibrated.

Mel111.beat: How far: one of the nearest clusters
Mel111.question: Why does one of the nearest star clusters look so loose and spread out?
Mel111.why: A cluster's apparent size is a nearness record of its own, and the Coma Star Cluster, among the closest families to the Sun, sprawls across most of a binocular field.
Mel111.look: Between Denebola and Cor Caroli a faint glittery patch to the eye becomes a sprawl of white stars across most of the binocular field. Its width on the sky is its distance speaking, while γ Comae, the orange star at its northern edge, is a foreground star and not part of the family.
Mel111.answer: At about 278 light-years its stars are spread over a patch some ten Moon-widths wide, and they are also drifting apart, so nearness and old age together make it look thin. Seen from ten times farther, the same family would shrink to a small knot and sink toward invisibility, so before any of its stars can be ranked by power, the distance has to come first.
Mel111.story: The Coma Star Cluster sits almost exactly toward the north pole of the galaxy, looking straight up out of the dusty disk, so its light reaches us nearly undimmed. That makes its distance one of the cleanest in the sky: parallaxes for its members agree with distances from their brightness without any correction for dust. Few clusters are so straightforward, and astronomers use clear sightlines like this one to check the corrections they must apply everywhere else.

IC2391.beat: How far: one of the nearest clusters
IC2391.question: How near is the bright little family around Omicron Velorum?
IC2391.why: A star family at a known distance is a ruler for every family farther out, and this one, among the nearest clusters to the Sun, spreads wider than the full Moon.
IC2391.look: Less than two degrees north of Delta Velorum, a corner of the False Cross, a knot of five or six naked-eye stars opens into a few dozen in binoculars. A family looks this loose and bright only from close by; the same stars from ten times farther would huddle into a small hazy spot.
IC2391.answer: The Omicron Velorum Cluster lies about 490 light-years away, which places it among the nearest clusters of all and explains why its members look bright and widely scattered. With the distance known, each member's brightness becomes a measure of its true power, and the blue-white stars at its heart turn out to outshine the Sun many times over.
IC2391.story: A cluster's distance is sturdier than any one star's because it is an average: Gaia measures the tiny yearly shift of every member, and pooling hundreds of them shrinks the error far below what a single star allows. That pooled distance then becomes a calibration, since the cluster's ordinary stars, now of known power, can be matched against the same kinds of star in clusters too far for parallax. Lining up the two families and reading the gap in brightness is how many farther clusters were first placed.

IC2602.beat: How far: one of the nearest clusters
IC2602.question: Why does the Southern Pleiades look so big and bright to the naked eye?
IC2602.why: Among the nearest star families to the Sun, the Southern Pleiades shows what nearness does to a cluster before any other record can be read.
IC2602.look: Find Theta Carinae, the brightest of a small spray of stars just south of the Carina Nebula. The eye counts five or six stars and binoculars two or three dozen, spread over about a degree, and that generous spread is the mark of a family on our doorstep.
IC2602.answer: Its stars lie only about 491 light-years away, so even modest members shine to the naked eye and the family spreads wider than the full Moon. Nearness is doing much of the work here, and only with the distance in hand can you ask how much light each of these stars really makes.
IC2602.story: Star families come in a fairly narrow range of true sizes, so how wide one looks is a rough gauge of how far it is, and the Southern Pleiades sprawl because they are near. In 1930 Robert Trumpler compared such size distances with distances from how faint each cluster's stars appeared, and found that the far clusters looked too faint for their size. Something between the stars was dimming their light, and that discovery of interstellar dust is a correction every distance record since has had to make.

Mel20.beat: How far: one of the nearest young clusters
Mel20.question: Why does this young star family fill your whole binocular field?
Mel20.why: Nearness changes how everything looks, and the Alpha Persei Cluster, one of the closest young families to the Sun, is the place to see that before chasing records farther out.
Mel20.look: Center Mirfak, the brightest star of Perseus, and let the field fill with the curving chains of blue-white stars around it. Most clusters on a star chart are small knots; this one overflows the view because it is one of the closest young families to the Sun.
Mel20.answer: It lies only about 566 light-years away, so its members scatter over several Moon-widths around Mirfak. With that distance known, Mirfak's glow becomes a true output far beyond the Sun's, and turning brightness into power this way is the step every later record needs.
Mel20.story: Distance dims a family as well as shrinking it. Each time the distance doubles, every member arrives four times fainter, so a family moved far enough to huddle into a knot also sinks into a faint grainy glow, Mirfak and all. Astronomers run this in reverse: they find the same kinds of star in a distant cluster, measure how much fainter they look, and read off how much farther it must lie.

HR2990.question: How close is the nearest giant star to the Sun?
HR2990.why: Giants are rare near the Sun, so the closest of them is a record holder, and its nearness is what lets astronomers take the measure of a star that has already swollen.
HR2990.look: Put Pollux and Castor in one field in Gemini: Pollux is the warm orange one, a giant late in life, while white Castor beside it is still in its long, steady prime.
HR2990.answer: Pollux lies about 33.8 light-years away, with Arcturus next among the giants at about 37. With the distance fixed, its glow becomes a real output of about 41 times the Sun's light, and that conversion from how bright to how powerful is the step every bigger record needs.
HR2990.story: Giants are scarce near the Sun for a simple reason of timing: a star spends only a small fraction of its life swollen, so at any moment only a few of its kind are caught in that stage. That scarcity is why the nearest giant lies several times farther than dozens of ordinary stars. Being near still pays, because a disk under a hundredth of an arcsecond wide is big enough for an interferometer to measure, and with the distance known that angle becomes a true width.

HR424.question: Why does it matter that the North Star is the nearest Cepheid?
HR424.why: The farthest records in the sky are measured with pulsing stars called Cepheids, and the whole method stands on the nearest of them, which happens to sit at the pole.
HR424.look: Follow the two end stars of the Big Dipper's bowl up to Polaris, at the tip of the Little Dipper's handle. It looks perfectly steady because its pulse is far too slight for the eye, and the little ring of fainter stars it sits on, the Engagement Ring, makes it easy to frame.
HR424.answer: Its distance, about 448 light-years, is close enough to measure directly, and it turns the North Star's modest glow into about 2,200 times the Sun's light. Pinning down the true power of a pulsing star like this one is what later lets the same kind of star measure distances far beyond any parallax.
HR424.story: A Cepheid ruler has two parts: the rule that slower pulsers are brighter, which can be read anywhere, and its zero point, which can only be set by Cepheids whose distances are measured directly. Polaris is the closest of those, yet careful studies of its distance have differed by roughly a quarter, enough to matter for the whole ruler. That argument is how the farthest records stay honest, for a galaxy's distance is only as firm as the nearby Cepheids it leans on.

STAR-Arcturus.beat: How far: the brightest northern star
STAR-Arcturus.question: Why is Arcturus the brightest star of the northern half of the sky?
STAR-Arcturus.why: Brightness is the record your eye judges on its own, so the brightest star north of the celestial equator is the place to ask how much of that brightness is mere nearness.
STAR-Arcturus.look: Follow the curve of the Big Dipper's handle away from the bowl to the first bright star, orange-gold Arcturus in Boötes. Nothing north of the celestial equator outshines it, and its warm color already hints that it is a cool, swollen giant.
STAR-Arcturus.answer: Closeness and power share the credit: at about 37 light-years it is one of the nearer bright stars, and as a swollen giant it outshines the Sun many times over. A star's glow in our sky always mixes those two, and with the distance settled, the power can at last be pulled out on its own.
STAR-Arcturus.story: Astronomers compare stars fairly by imagining each one moved to a standard distance of about 33 light-years and quoting the brightness it would have there. Arcturus happens to sit only a little beyond that mark, so its brightness in our sky is nearly its standard brightness, and what you see is close to a fair measure of its power. Sirius, moved out to the same mark, would fade to about the brightness of Regulus, while Rigel would outshine everything in the night sky except the Moon.

HR2326.question: Is Canopus bright because it is near, like Sirius, or for another reason?
HR2326.why: Second place in the brightness record goes to Canopus, and the gap between its distance and that of Sirius, the winner, is the best puzzle in the sky about what that record measures.
HR2326.look: Canopus needs no finder: it is the brilliant white star well south of Sirius, in Carina. Sweep about 6° west to faint Beta Pictoris, a star five times closer, and you have brightness and nearness pointing in opposite directions.
HR2326.answer: Canopus is bright for the opposite reason to Sirius, since it is about 36 times farther away and so must be several hundred times more powerful to come so close in our sky. Brightness can hide two opposite stories, and only once a distance says which one a star is telling can its true power be read.
HR2326.story: For most of the twentieth century nobody knew how far Canopus was, and published estimates ranged from about a hundred light-years to more than a thousand, so its power could have been anything from modest to colossal. The Hipparcos satellite, measuring parallax above the blur of the atmosphere, finally pinned the yearly shift down to about a hundredth of an arcsecond, and only then did its brightness become a firm number. A record for power is never stronger than the distance underneath it, and Canopus spent decades as the sky's best example.

HD95735.beat: How far: a near red dwarf you cannot see
HD95735.question: How can the brightest red dwarf in the northern sky still need binoculars?
HD95735.why: Most of the Sun's neighbors are red dwarfs, and the brightest of them in the northern sky shows how far brightness and nearness can drift apart.
HD95735.look: Below the Big Dipper's bowl, about four and a half degrees south of 47 Ursae Majoris, a chart picks out a dim, faintly orange point. Sirius, which blazes in the winter sky, lies a little farther away than this.
HD95735.answer: It gives out only about a thirtieth of the Sun's light, so even from about 8.3 light-years, a little nearer than Sirius, it stays below naked-eye view. The sky's bright stars are rare, powerful ones seen from afar, and only their distances can say how much light they truly make.
HD95735.story: Turning a faint point into a true output takes two steps: measure how much light arrives across all wavelengths, then scale it up by the square of the distance. For a red dwarf the first step holds a surprise, because its cool surface sends most of its energy out as infrared, and the eye catches only a thin slice of an already modest output. In visible light alone it falls nearly two hundred times short of the Sun, so the figure the eye would guess and the figure the instruments give are very far apart.

HD202560.beat: How far: the brightest red dwarf
HD202560.question: If the brightest red dwarf in the sky is this faint, what about the rest?
HD202560.why: Red dwarfs are the commonest stars in the galaxy, and the record for the brightest of them all belongs to this faint orange point in Microscopium.
HD202560.look: About twenty degrees west-south-west of Fomalhaut, in Microscopium, a faint, slightly orange point sits among other faint stars, so use the chart to be sure. From mid-northern sites it stays low and rewards a clear southern horizon.
HD202560.answer: The rest are fainter still: Lacaille 8760 gives out about a ninth of the Sun's light and sits just below naked-eye reach from only about 13 light-years. Brightness in our sky is a poor guide to what stars are like, so the powerful stars that dominate it have to be weighed with their distances attached.
HD202560.story: Astronomers learned how misleading the bright sky is by counting stars out to a fixed distance instead of down to a fixed brightness. Inside a sphere a few dozen light-years across, roughly three stars in four turn out to be red dwarfs, and hardly any of them can be seen without optics. A count by brightness gets it the other way round, filled with rare powerful stars gathered from enormous volumes of space, which is why a record like this one has to be read with its distance attached.

M42.beat: How far: the nearest heavy-star nursery
M42.question: How far away is the nearest place still making heavy stars?
M42.why: The heaviest stars are born in only a few places, and the nearest of these nurseries hangs in Orion's Sword, close enough for its distance to be measured well.
M42.look: Find the three-star Sword below Orion's Belt; its middle star looks fuzzy even to the eye. Binoculars show gray wings of glowing gas around a bright knot, and that knot is where the heaviest newborn stars sit.
M42.answer: The Orion Nebula, the nearest of them, lies more than a hundred times farther than Sirius, which is why the heaviest stars never look as bright as they really are. Once that distance is known, the bright knot at the nebula's heart can be weighed in light, and it turns out to hold some of the most powerful stars in this part of the galaxy.
M42.story: Heavy stars are rare from birth: for every star of twenty Suns a cloud makes something like five hundred smaller ones, and only giant clouds make them at all. So the nurseries of the hottest stars are few and far apart, and the nearest one active today is this one. Being the nearest makes it the reference for the rest, because the spectra of its young heavyweights, studied close up, are how astronomers recognize the same kind of star when it is too distant and too buried to study well.

HR3165.beat: How hot: one of the hottest stars you can see
HR3165.question: How hot is one of the hottest stars your eyes can see?
HR3165.why: Naos sits near the top of the color thermometer, among the hottest surfaces the naked eye can reach, so it is the place to see what a star's color can and cannot say.
HR3165.answer: Naos's surface runs at about 40,000 K, close to seven times the Sun's, yet it looks only steely blue-white. Past a certain heat a star's visible color stops changing and the rest of its glare pours out as ultraviolet. Each square meter that hot shines thousands of times more fiercely than the Sun's, so a star like this needs surprisingly little surface to be enormously powerful.
HR3165.story: Most of Naos's light never reaches the ground, because the air absorbs ultraviolet, so the full measure of its heat had to wait for telescopes in orbit. Instruments in space recorded that ultraviolet directly and found it crossed by lines of highly charged atoms streaming outward in a fast wind, a wind driven by the very light whose heat it reveals. Joining that ultraviolet to the visible spectrum is how the top of the temperature scale was finally tied down.

HD192163.beat: How hot: one of the hottest exposed surfaces
HD192163.question: How can a plain white point in Cygnus have a 70,000-degree surface?
HD192163.why: Among the hottest surfaces binoculars can reach is this plain point in Cygnus, a heavy star stripped down to its scorching interior.
HD192163.look: Drift about 2.7° south-west of Sadr, the star at the heart of the Northern Cross, and use the chart to pick out a plain white point among the Milky Way stars. Its color gives nothing away, which is the lesson of the hottest stars: past a certain heat the eye sees only white, while most of the light has moved into the ultraviolet.
HD192163.answer: Strip a heavy star of its hydrogen and what remains is hotter than any ordinary surface, nearly twice as hot as Naos, one of the hottest stars the naked eye can see. It looks faint and plainly white because it lies far away and sends most of its energy out as ultraviolet, and a surface this fierce means the star itself can be small, a size only its power and heat together can reveal.
HD192163.story: A Wolf-Rayet star hides its own surface inside a dense, fast wind, so its temperature cannot simply be read off like an ordinary star's. Astronomers model the wind and check the result against the gas around it, because the Crescent Nebula glows only where the star's ultraviolet is energetic enough to strip electrons from its atoms. How hard that stripping is, shown by which elements lose how many electrons, is a thermometer read at second hand from light the eye never sees.

HR8622.beat: How hot: the standard for the hottest stars
HR8622.question: Why does one of the hottest stars you can see look only faintly blue?
HR8622.why: The hottest stars set the top of the color thermometer, and 10 Lacertae is so standard an example that astronomers use it to define its class.
HR8622.look: Lacerta's faint zigzag lies between Cygnus and Andromeda, and 10 Lacertae sits at its southern end. Look for at best a hint of blue in a plain white point; for a star with one of the hottest surfaces you can see, that faint tint is all the eye can register.
HR8622.answer: Most of its light is ultraviolet, and the visible part that reaches you has nearly the same blue-white tint as stars far cooler, so the eye's thermometer simply runs out of scale. The spectrum still gives the heat, and heat says how much light each square meter sends out, which is half of what it takes to work out how big the star is.
HR8622.story: Past about twenty thousand degrees, a star's visible light comes from the long, gently sloping tail of its glow, where the balance of blue and red barely changes however much hotter the surface gets. Double the temperature of such a star and its color shifts by only a shade, while its ultraviolet soars. That is why astronomers rank the hottest stars by their spectral lines, the way this star's own lines set the standard for its type.

HR1879.beat: How hot: the hottest class of star
HR1879.question: How hot is the star at the head of Orion?
HR1879.why: Orion is full of hot blue stars, and the little triangle at its head holds one from the hottest class of all, a fair place to calibrate the thermometer.
HR1879.look: At Orion's head, above and between Betelgeuse and Bellatrix, binoculars turn a faint smudge into a small triangle of stars. The brightest is Meissa, a crisp blue-white, and its color is the first, rough reading of a very hot surface.
HR1879.answer: Meissa's surface runs at about 35,200 K, some six times the Sun's, a figure read from lines in its spectrum that only very hot gas can produce. In binoculars that heat comes through as nothing more than a crisp blue-white, yet it fixes how much light each square meter sends out, and from there a star's power gives away how much surface it must have.
HR1879.story: Meissa is one of the reference stars for its spectral type, a star whose spectrum others are compared against when they are sorted into classes. The sorting itself is a thermometer: the classes from O through M follow falling temperature, and within each class a number marks finer steps, so placing a new star means finding the standard its lines match best. Hot standards like this one anchor the top of the scale, where the eye's judgment of color has long since given out.

DS-15Mon.beat: How hot: the hottest class of star
DS-15Mon.question: How hot is the star at the foot of the Christmas Tree Cluster?
DS-15Mon.why: The Christmas Tree Cluster's brightest star belongs to the hottest class there is, and the gap between its color and Betelgeuse's, on the way there, is a temperature gap you can see.
DS-15Mon.look: Sweep about 11° east of Betelgeuse to the small, upside-down triangle of the Christmas Tree Cluster, with 15 Monocerotis as the bright star at its base. Compare its crisp white light with orange Betelgeuse on the way: the color gap between them is a temperature gap of tens of thousands of degrees.
DS-15Mon.answer: Published values run from about 25,000 to 45,000 K, a reminder that even the thermometer has error bars when a star sits inside a cloud of its own glowing gas. Either way each square meter of it outshines the Sun's many times over, so its power needs far less surface than a cool star's would.
DS-15Mon.story: For the hottest stars the thermometer is a balance between spectral lines. Helium that still holds both its electrons absorbs at some colors, helium stripped of one absorbs at others, and the hotter the surface, the more the stripped kind wins, so the ratio places a star on the scale. The same balance defines the hottest class itself, the O stars, and 15 Monocerotis is a member in good standing.

HR5191.beat: How hot: the hottest Big Dipper star
HR5191.question: Which of the seven Big Dipper stars is the hottest, and how can you tell?
HR5191.why: The Big Dipper is a ready-made thermometer test, seven bright stars under one sky with a single winner for heat at the end of the handle.
HR5191.look: Sweep from Dubhe, at the far corner of the bowl, along the handle to Alkaid at its tip. Dubhe has a yellow-orange cast, Alkaid a crisp blue-white, and the five stars between are plain white, so the whole Dipper spans the color scale in one sweep.
HR5191.answer: Alkaid wins, and your eye can call the result before any spectrograph does: the bluer the tint, the hotter the surface, and nothing in the Dipper is bluer. Heat says how much light pours from each square meter, so once a star's power is known as well, the only thing left to find is how many square meters it has.
HR5191.story: Ranking by color works because every glowing surface follows the same curve: as the temperature climbs, the peak of its light slides from red through yellow toward blue, so the balance between blue and red light tells the heat. A poker in a fire, a stove ring and a lightbulb filament obey the same rule, and so do the stars of the Dipper. Measured through two colored filters, the Dipper's seven stars line up in an order that puts Dubhe at the warm end and Alkaid at the cold one, as your eye does.

HR4199.beat: How hot: the hottest star of its family
HR4199.question: Which star leads the Southern Pleiades in heat, and how hot is it?
HR4199.why: Inside one family every star shares a distance, so its brightest member is also its most powerful, and Theta Carinae's crisp blue-white says how much of that power is heat.
HR4199.look: Theta Carinae is the brightest of the loose group of blue-white stars just south of the Carina Nebula. In binoculars its color is the crispest in the field, and since its neighbors share its distance, its lead in brightness is a lead in heat and power.
HR4199.answer: Theta Carinae leads the family at about 31,300 K, more than five times the Sun's surface temperature. That heat is also why it is the family's brightest member, and since each square meter of it outshines the Sun's hundreds of times over, its power needs only a small body.
HR4199.story: In a young cluster the members line up along a single sequence on a chart of color against brightness, hotter stars brighter, because a star's mass sets both. Theta Carinae sits at the top of that sequence, which is why heat and brightness point at the same star. By some reckonings it is also a blue straggler, a star that may have gained mass from a partner and so looks younger and hotter than its family's age allows.

HR1607.beat: How cold: one of the reddest stars
HR1607.question: Is the reddest star in binocular reach also the coolest one?
HR1607.why: At the cold end of the thermometer the color record and the temperature record nearly coincide, and Hind's Crimson Star sits near the bottom of both.
HR1607.answer: Hind's Crimson Star comes close, for its surface is among the coolest of any star you can find with binoculars, yet carbon soot in its atmosphere deepens the red further still, so its color overstates the chill. A surface that cool gives out little light from each square meter, so for the star to be seen from about 1,500 light-years at all, it must have an enormous number of them.
HR1607.story: Hind's Crimson Star does not hold its color steadily. Over its slow cycle of swelling and shrinking its surface cools as it dims, and the cooler gas forms more of the carbon molecules and soot that strip out blue light, so it looks reddest near its faintest. John Russell Hind, who noticed it in 1845, compared it to a drop of blood, and observers still try to catch it near minimum, when its color record is at its strongest.

NAME-TLyrae.beat: How cold: one of the reddest stars
NAME-TLyrae.question: How can a star beside Vega look redder than almost anything in binocular range?
NAME-TLyrae.why: Vega and T Lyrae share one binocular field and sit at opposite ends of the color record, which makes them the cleanest color test in the northern sky.
NAME-TLyrae.answer: At about 2,400 K its surface is among the coolest measured, but most of the redness is a filter, carbon molecules in its atmosphere stripping out the blue. Even so, a surface that cool sheds only a sliver of the Sun's light from each square meter, so a star still visible from well over a thousand light-years must be vast.
NAME-TLyrae.story: The two stars are linked by more than the field. Vega is the star astronomers chose as the zero of the color scale: by definition it is equally bright through the blue filter and the yellow one, and every other star's color index is how far it departs from Vega. T Lyrae departs about as far as any star binoculars can show, so in one view you are looking at the scale's origin and very nearly its far end.

HR9004.beat: How cold: one of the reddest naked-eye stars
HR9004.question: What gives one of the reddest naked-eye stars its color?
HR9004.why: The cold end of the color record belongs to carbon stars, and TX Piscium is one of the few bright enough to see without optics.
HR9004.answer: Its surface is cool enough to glow orange on its own, and the spare carbon in its atmosphere then filters out the blue and violet, leaving a deep ruddy red. A star that cool can only be seen from about 800 light-years because it gives out thousands of Suns' worth of light, and a cool surface can manage that only by being immense.
HR9004.story: TX Piscium is near enough for its disk to be measured, and that gives a temperature the soot cannot fool. An interferometer finds the disk's width on the sky, instruments across the infrared collect all the light the star sends, and the law that ties a glowing body's output to its size and heat says how hot a surface that wide must be to give off that much. Done this way the answer does not depend on color at all, and it confirms that the reddest naked-eye stars really are among the coolest.

STAR-LaSuperba.beat: How cold: a rare naked-eye carbon star
STAR-LaSuperba.question: How cool is the star Angelo Secchi named the superb one?
STAR-LaSuperba.why: Temperature records at the cold end are written in red, and La Superba, one of the very few carbon stars the unaided eye can catch, writes it boldly.
STAR-LaSuperba.answer: La Superba's surface runs at less than half the Sun's temperature, which puts it near the cold end of all the stars you can see. A surface that cool sheds little light per square meter, so for La Superba to reach your eye from about 800 light-years it must be spread over a vast area, and how vast takes its power and its temperature together.
STAR-LaSuperba.story: Angelo Secchi, sorting several thousand stars by their spectra in the 1860s, set the red stars with strange dark bands apart in a class of their own, and this was the finest example he found, hence the name. His classes were the first step toward reading temperature from starlight, long before anyone could say what the bands meant. They are now known to be carbon molecules, and the star's place at the cold end follows from the physics that Secchi's sorting first hinted at.

HR3541.beat: How cold: red beside the Beehive
HR3541.question: Why does X Cancri stand out from the Beehive's white stars by color alone?
HR3541.why: Color records are easiest to judge beside a neutral reference, and X Cancri sits a few degrees from the Beehive, one of the redder stars within binocular reach.
HR3541.answer: It is cool and sooty at once, so its light starts out orange and then loses its blue on the way out, while the white stars around it are thousands of degrees hotter. A surface that cool gives out little light per square meter, so a star this far away that still shows up in binoculars must be spread over an enormous area.
HR3541.story: Astronomers turned the eye's color judgment into a number by measuring stars through a blue filter and a yellow one and taking the difference. For ordinary stars that difference rises smoothly as the surface cools, from slightly below zero for the hottest to near plus two for the coolest ordinary giants, so it reads like a thermometer scale. X Cancri runs well past the end of it, because carbon in its atmosphere removes blue light that temperature alone would leave, and the number overstates the chill.

HR7220.beat: How cold: a deep-red carbon star
HR7220.question: How cool is the vividly red star in southern Aquila?
HR7220.why: The summer sky's cold end is held by a handful of carbon stars, and V Aquilae is the easiest of them to catch beside a white neighbor.
HR7220.answer: V Aquilae's surface sits at about 2,600 K, less than half the Sun's temperature, and its carbon makes it look redder still. A surface that cool must be enormous to be seen from about 1,400 light-years, and how enormous follows from setting its power against its heat.
HR7220.story: Carbon stars were recognized by their spectra long before anyone knew why they existed. Their light is crossed by bands from molecules of two carbon atoms, the same bands that give a candle flame's base its blue and many comets their green glow, and the strength of those bands sets a star's place in the carbon sequence. The reason came only with the physics of late stellar life: deep shell flashes make the carbon, and churning currents carry it up.

HR1648.question: Which star in Orion runs even cooler than Betelgeuse?
HR1648.why: Betelgeuse is famous for its cool red glow, yet a much fainter star near Bellatrix runs cooler still, the best place in Orion to read the cold end of the thermometer.
HR1648.look: About 7° south-west of Bellatrix, Orion's western shoulder, look for an orange-red star among white field stars; a slight defocus boosts the color. Then glance at Betelgeuse: the famous red star looks paler orange beside this one, though it is far brighter.
HR1648.answer: W Orionis is roughly 900 degrees cooler than Betelgeuse at the surface, and the carbon in its atmosphere reddens it further. Each square meter that cool gives out only about a twentieth of the Sun's light, so a red star still visible in binoculars from well over a thousand light-years must be huge, as Betelgeuse is.
HR1648.story: Betelgeuse and W Orionis are cool in different chemistries. In Betelgeuse oxygen outnumbers carbon, so its spectrum is striped with bands of titanium oxide; in W Orionis carbon has won, and bands of carbon molecules take their place. Each set of bands deepens in a known way as the gas cools, which is how two red stars of different makeup can still be put on one thermometer.

HR2405.beat: How cold: the carbon star of Auriga
HR2405.question: How cool is the orange-red star glowing between Capella and Gemini?
HR2405.why: Every color record needs a star whose temperature has actually been measured, and UU Aurigae, a carbon star in eastern Auriga, gives the winter sky a cold reading you can see.
HR2405.look: Between Capella and the Gemini twins, in eastern Auriga, one star among the white ones glows orange-red. Judge it with short glances, then swing to golden Capella to set the two colors side by side.
HR2405.answer: UU Aurigae's surface runs roughly half as hot as the Sun's, which is cold for a star, and its carbon pushes the color deeper red than heat alone would. At half the Sun's temperature each square meter gives out only about a sixteenth of the Sun's light, so a star bright enough to see from about 1,600 light-years must make up for it with an enormous surface.
HR2405.story: Your eye is an awkward thermometer at night. The cells that see color need a fair amount of light, while the night-vision cells that take over in the dark see only gray, so a star's tint shows best when it is bright enough to wake the color cells. Red stars add a twist, since if stared at for long they seem to gain on white neighbors, which is why observers judge them in short glances and why astronomers trust instruments, not eyes, for the number.

HR8297.beat: How cold: a bright summer carbon star
HR8297.question: How cool is one of the brightest carbon stars of the summer sky?
HR8297.why: Carbon stars hold the cold end of the color record, and V460 Cygni is bright enough to show it in almost any binoculars.
HR8297.answer: V460 Cygni's surface sits at about 2,850 K, roughly half the Sun's temperature, and the carbon it has dredged up reddens its glow further. From about 1,900 light-years a star that cool reaches binoculars only by pouring out a great deal of light from a vast surface, and its power and heat together say how vast.
HR8297.story: A carbon star has no sharp surface. Its atmosphere fades out over a depth comparable to its own width, and the light we receive comes from different layers at different colors, so there is no single place to hold the thermometer. Astronomers define its temperature as that of a simple glowing ball with the same size and total output, and it is that figure, not any one layer's, that places a cool star on the record.

HR9045.question: How big must a faint yellow star be to outshine half a million Suns?
HR9045.why: ρ Cassiopeiae looks like a faint yellowish star beside Caph, yet its power is among the greatest the eye can reach, and its plain color is what turns that power into a size.
HR9045.look: Start at Caph, the western end of Cassiopeia's W, and slide about two and a half degrees west-south-west to a faint yellowish star. Nothing in the view says that this is one of the most powerful stars your eye will ever catch, and its yellow, close to the Sun's own tint, is the clue that sizes it.
HR9045.answer: Its yellow says the surface runs nearly as hot as the Sun's, so each square meter shines about as brightly, and the only way to pour out some 676,000 Suns' worth of light is to have that much more surface. Measurements put it at about 630 times the Sun's width, a heavy star swollen near the end of its life, and since heavy stars burn out first, swollen giants like this are already a kind of clock.
HR9045.story: Rho Cassiopeiae sits in an awkward place for a star so luminous, a band of temperatures where the outer layers of a swollen hypergiant turn unstable. Every few decades it seems to bounce off that boundary, cooling and dimming as it throws off a shell, then warming again, and astronomers caught such episodes in the 1940s and more than once in recent decades. Its size is therefore a moving target, swelling and shrinking a little with each episode.

STAR-Deneb.beat: How much light: the Summer Triangle's powerhouse
STAR-Deneb.question: How much more powerful is Deneb than Vega, the brighter-looking star?
STAR-Deneb.why: With distances known, the Summer Triangle's three corners can be ranked by the light they really make, and the faintest-looking corner wins by a margin the eye would never guess.
STAR-Deneb.look: Deneb marks the tail of Cygnus and the faintest-looking corner of the Summer Triangle. Hold it in the field, then glance at Vega, plainly brighter: you are comparing a nearby lamp with a lighthouse seen from across a sea.
STAR-Deneb.answer: Deneb pours out about 196,000 Suns' worth of light against Vega's roughly 51, close to four thousand times as much. A star can make that much light by running very hot or by being very large, and the number alone cannot say which.
STAR-Deneb.story: When parallax runs out, a star's spectrum can still vouch for its power. A supergiant's outer layers are so thin and so loosely held that its absorption lines come out unusually narrow, a trait Antonia Maury flagged in the 1890s and Ejnar Hertzsprung soon recognized as the mark of the most luminous stars. Deneb's lines are as narrow as they come, which places it among the brightest class of stars whatever its exact distance turns out to be.

HR6262.beat: How much light: the faint star that wins
HR6262.question: How powerful is the fainter star of the pair in Scorpius' tail?
HR6262.why: Two stars sit side by side in the Scorpion's tail, and once their distances are known, the record for power goes to the one that looks fainter.
HR6262.answer: ζ¹ pours out about 851,000 Suns' worth of light, which makes it one of the most luminous stars the eye can see and one of the most massive in the Milky Way, about 36 Suns by one estimate. Power on that scale has to come from a fiercely hot surface, a vast one or both, and the light itself has to say which.
HR6262.story: ζ¹ Scorpii's own parallax is too small to measure well, so it borrows a distance from its family, the compact young cluster just to its north, whose many members pin down the range together. Dust along the way then has to be subtracted, since it dims the star by well over a magnitude and tints it toward pale yellow-white, and the size of the tint tells how much light was lost. Distance, dust and brightness together turn a modest-looking point into one of the galaxy's beacons.

HR1713.beat: How much light: a powerhouse at Orion's foot
HR1713.question: How much light must Rigel pour out to rival Sirius from a hundred times farther?
HR1713.why: Brightness alone would crown Sirius, but once distances are known the power record looks very different, and Rigel, Orion's blue-white foot, is where the difference shows.
HR1713.look: Rigel is Orion's brilliant blue-white foot, diagonally across from Betelgeuse. Sirius, low to the south-east, outshines it only a few times over, even though Rigel lies about a hundred times farther away.
HR1713.answer: Rigel pours out about 83,000 times the Sun's light, thousands of times what Sirius manages, and nothing less would let it come so close to Sirius in our sky across a hundred times the distance. That number says how much light leaves the star but not how, by a hotter surface or a bigger one, and color is the clue that tells them apart.
HR1713.story: The arithmetic behind that number is the inverse-square law: light spreading from a star thins out over the surface of an ever larger sphere, so at three times the distance each square meter of your eye receives nine times less. Run the law backward with Rigel's measured faintness and distance and out comes its output, after one more correction for the ultraviolet the eye misses. The step is simple, but every power record on this ladder is built from it.

HR6736.beat: How much light: the lamp of the Lagoon
HR6736.question: How heavy are the stars that light the Lagoon Nebula?
HR6736.why: Power climbs steeply with mass, and the lamp inside the Lagoon Nebula, once its distance is known, turns out to be a pair of true heavyweights.
HR6736.answer: The heavier of the two holds over 50 Suns' worth of matter, and that weight is the engine of the pair's enormous output, enough to light up much of the nebula around it. Weight explains how much light a star makes, and how hot its surface must run to let all that light out is the next thing its light can tell.
HR6736.story: Heavy stars rarely live alone: surveys of the hottest stars find that most have a close companion, and more than two in three will swap matter with it at some point. That is a gift for the record books, because a pair is the only way to weigh a star directly, through its orbit. It also means many of the heaviest stars do not end as they began, since a partner can strip one star or feed the other.

HD226868.beat: How much light: a giant beside a black hole
HD226868.question: What can be as heavy as twenty Suns and give off no light?
HD226868.why: Behind every power record stands a mass, and here the mass can be weighed twice, once in a visible giant star and once in the dark object it circles.
HD226868.answer: The dark partner is a black hole, the collapsed core of a massive star, and Cygnus X-1 was the first X-ray source widely accepted as one. Its visible partner, about 40 Suns' worth of star, pours out hundreds of thousands of Suns' worth of light, and whether that light comes from heat or from size is something only its spectrum can settle.
HD226868.story: The case rested on a minimum weight. The visible star's swing, timed from the Doppler shifts in its spectrum, sets a lower limit on the mass of whatever pulls it, and once the giant's own weight was estimated, the unseen partner came out heavier than any neutron star can be. Nothing that heavy and that dark could be an ordinary star, and Stephen Hawking, who had bet against the black hole, conceded in 1990.

HR4210.beat: How much light: a star near its limit
HR4210.question: Why does one of the most massive stars known look so modest tonight?
HR4210.why: At the top of the power records sit stars so heavy they can barely hold together, and Eta Carinae, a star that once nearly tore itself apart in a great eruption, is the most famous of them.
HR4210.answer: It hides behind its own wreckage, for the gas it threw off in the 1840s has cooled into dust that dims and reddens the star. Underneath, it is so luminous that its own light nearly overpowers its gravity, and because the dust hides its true color, how hot that buried surface runs is far harder to read than how much light it makes.
HR4210.story: The dust that hides Eta Carinae also gives its power away. The starlight it absorbs warms it, and it glows in the infrared, so adding up that infrared glow recovers nearly the whole output of the hidden star. Measured this way it comes to several million Suns, and in the late 1960s this patch of sky turned out to be the brightest source of mid-infrared light beyond the solar system.

HR7763.beat: How much light: a heavyweight on a knife edge
HR7763.question: Why does a star as powerful as P Cygni live on a knife edge?
HR7763.why: Past a certain power a star's own light starts to push it apart, and P Cygni, a luminous blue variable, sits right on that edge.
HR7763.look: From Sadr, at the center of the Northern Cross, slide about 2½° south-west toward Albireo to a plain white point against the Milky Way. That faint, steady glow, reaching you from more than 5,000 light-years, is the measure of its power.
HR7763.answer: P Cygni makes nearly as much light as a star of its weight can make and still keep its outer layers, so its grip on them keeps slipping, and in 1600 it slipped far enough to flare to third magnitude. Whether all that light pours from heat or from sheer surface is a question its color can start to answer.
HR7763.story: P Cygni gave its name to a line shape that astronomers now look for in every windy star. Its spectral lines show bright emission from gas flowing out on all sides, with a dark notch on the blue edge where gas rushing toward us absorbs the star's light, and the width of that notch gives the wind's speed. Reading the same shape in distant stars is how astronomers measure how fast the heaviest stars are losing themselves.

HR3207.beat: How much light: a pair with a stripped star
HR3207.question: What has Gamma Velorum's power already cost its smaller star?
HR3207.why: Weighing a star needs a partner swinging around it, and the brightest point of Vela is just such a pair, one of them already changed by its own power.
HR3207.answer: Its own fierce winds blew away its hydrogen, so what remains is the hot inner core of a once much heavier star. Power on this scale has a cost, since the stars that shine hardest also lose themselves fastest, and a star stripped to its core runs hotter than any color the eye can judge.
HR3207.story: Light pushes. Each photon carries a tiny momentum, and in the outer layers of a star this luminous, atoms soak up so many of them that the gas is driven off in a wind moving well over a thousand kilometers a second. Over a few million years such a wind can strip away much of a star's mass, and Gamma Velorum's Wolf-Rayet member, the brightest of its kind in the sky, is what remains after that stripping.

HR2782.beat: How much light: one knot outshines a cluster
HR2782.question: How can one knot of stars outshine its entire cluster?
HR2782.why: Power climbs steeply with mass, and once the cluster's distance is known, τ Canis Majoris shows it at a glance, one bright point drowning out the family around it.
HR2782.answer: A few very heavy stars in one spot give out more light than all the lighter members together, enough to reach naked-eye brightness from about 4,000 light-years. That much light can come from a blazing surface or from a huge one, and the blue-white of this knot already hints which.
HR2782.story: The rule behind it is one of the steepest in astronomy: for stars in their steady adult life, output climbs roughly as the third or fourth power of mass. Double a star's mass and it shines about ten times brighter; make it twenty times heavier than the Sun and it outshines the Sun tens of thousands of times. The rule was found by weighing stars in pairs, from their orbits, and comparing their light, and this field shows its consequence at a glance.

HR2827.beat: How much light: winter's hidden powerhouse
HR2827.question: How much light does the star at the tip of the Great Dog's tail give out?
HR2827.why: Power records depend on distance, and Aludra, one of the mightiest stars of the winter sky, shows how much an uncertain distance can move the total.
HR2827.look: Aludra is the blue-white star at the tip of the Great Dog's tail, south-east of Sirius. It looks like a supporting player beside Sirius, and only its distance, roughly two hundred times greater, says otherwise.
HR2827.answer: Aludra gives out about 40,000 times the Sun's light by one estimate, though its distance spans roughly 1,600 to 2,600 light-years and power grows with the square of it. Even at the low end it outshines Sirius around a thousand times over, and its crisp blue-white color hints that much of that power comes from heat.
HR2827.story: Measuring Aludra's parallax is harder than its brightness suggests. Its yearly shift is close to the limit of the Hipparcos satellite, and Gaia, far more precise for fainter stars, handles stars this bright poorly, because their light overflows its detectors. So the power of one of winter's mightiest stars still hangs on an older, rougher measurement, and the honest way to quote it is as a range.

HR1895.beat: How much light: the Orion Nebula's power plant
HR1895.question: Which single star system lights most of the Orion Nebula?
HR1895.why: A nebula's glow is a meter for the power of the stars inside it, and once the nebula's distance is known, that meter points to one bright knot in the core.
HR1895.answer: θ¹ Orionis C does, a heavyweight pair at the heart of the nebula that supplies most of the ultraviolet keeping the cloud alight. Ultraviolet that strong can only pour from a very hot surface, so here the power record already points to the next number, a temperature, which a star's color is the first way to read.
HR1895.story: Every hydrogen atom the star strips must sooner or later recapture an electron and glow, so the nebula's total hydrogen light, or its radio glow, counts how many atom-stripping photons the star pours out each second. That count is a measure of power in the ultraviolet, where the eye sees nothing, and for the Orion Nebula it points to one star of the hottest kind. Astronomers use the same bookkeeping on nebulae in other galaxies to weigh up stars they cannot see one by one.

HR5056.beat: How much light: Virgo's brightest star
HR5056.question: How powerful is the brightest star in Virgo?
HR5056.why: Within one constellation the brightness record is a fair place to start measuring power, and Virgo's goes to Spica, a lone blue-white light whose distance is well known.
HR5056.answer: Spica gives out about 20,500 times the Sun's light from about 250 light-years, most of it from the heavier of its two hot stars. A star can earn that output with heat or with size, and Spica's icy blue-white is the first clue to which.
HR5056.story: Spica's two stars are far too close to split in any ordinary telescope, yet the pair has been weighed, one of the first to be done this way. In the early 1970s an instrument in Australia that compared the flicker of starlight at two separate mirrors traced the orbit on the sky, while the shifting lines in the spectrum gave the speeds, and together they fixed the masses and the distance at once. With mass and distance in hand the power follows, and it confirms what the mass predicts.

STAR-MuCep.beat: How big: one of the largest naked-eye stars
STAR-MuCep.question: How wide is one of the largest stars you can see without optics?
STAR-MuCep.why: The Garnet Star is cool, deep red and still bright from far beyond the Sun's neighborhood, the combination that can only mean an enormous surface.
STAR-MuCep.answer: The Garnet Star spans somewhere between about 600 and 1,300 times the Sun's width, depending on its still-uncertain distance, which makes it one of the largest stars in the naked-eye sky. Stars swell like this only after a heavy core has burned through its hydrogen, and because heavier stars get there sooner, which stars have already swollen or vanished is a way of telling time.
STAR-MuCep.story: The Garnet Star's own parallax is too small and too unsteady to trust, since its vast, churning surface makes the center of its light wander, so its distance is usually borrowed from the group of young hot stars in Cepheus it travels with. That borrowed distance scales everything else: double it and the star's width doubles too. Its place in the size record therefore comes as a range, and it will narrow only as the family's distance does.

HR8383.beat: How big: a giant with an eclipsing partner
HR8383.question: How wide is the giant star that hides its partner for over a year?
HR8383.why: Sizes usually come from power and heat, but VV Cephei offers a second ruler, a partner star that disappears behind the giant every twenty years.
HR8383.answer: VV Cephei spans about 779 times the Sun's width, measured with an interferometer, which places it among the largest stars binoculars can show in the northern sky. Like every star near the top of this list it is a heavy star swollen in old age, and since heavy stars swell and die first, the giants a crowd has or has lost are a record of its age.
HR8383.story: Eclipses of this kind also let astronomers probe the giant from the inside. Before and after the full eclipse the blue star shines through the giant's thin outer layers, and its light picks up absorption from gas at one height after another, like a lamp seen through a thickening fog. Those spectra show how gradually the giant's edge fades away, which is why a supergiant's width depends on which layer one decides to call its surface.

HD212466.beat: How big: one of the largest stars known
HD212466.question: Can binoculars show one of the largest stars in the whole galaxy?
HD212466.why: The galaxy's size record is shared by a few swollen supergiants, and one of them sits in southern Cepheus, plain and orange in binoculars.
HD212466.look: About two and a half degrees south-south-west of δ Cephei, binoculars show a modest orange point. The orange says cool, and a cool star that reaches binocular brightness from deep across the Milky Way can only be doing it with a vast surface.
HD212466.answer: RW Cephei is among the largest stars known anywhere in the Milky Way, and it looks this ordinary only because it lies so far away, deep in the dusty disk of the galaxy. Like all such giants it is a heavy star near its end, and that link between weight and a short life is what lets astronomers read the age of whole crowds of stars.
HD212466.story: There seems to be a ceiling on how big a star can get. Surveys of the most luminous stars find no cool supergiants above a certain output, a boundary named for Roberta Humphreys and Kris Davidson, because the very heaviest stars lose their outer layers in winds and eruptions before they can swell that far. The size record therefore belongs to stars just under that boundary, such as this one, and not to the heaviest stars of all.

STAR-Betelgeuse.beat: How big: the most famous giant
STAR-Betelgeuse.question: Is Betelgeuse the largest star you can see, or only the most famous?
STAR-Betelgeuse.why: Orion's red shoulder is cool yet brilliant, exactly the mix that forces an enormous surface, and it is the size record most people know.
STAR-Betelgeuse.answer: It is one of the largest the naked eye can reach, but not the champion: VY Canis Majoris, a binocular star in the Great Dog, is nearly twice as wide, and the Garnet Star may also be bigger. Like them, Betelgeuse is a heavy star swollen late in life, and because heavy stars burn out first, which of them a crowd still holds tells how old the crowd is.
STAR-Betelgeuse.story: Betelgeuse was the first star beyond the Sun whose width was ever measured. In 1920 Albert Michelson and Francis Pease mounted a steel beam across the top of the great Mount Wilson telescope, with mirrors that could be slid apart along it, and watched the interference pattern vanish when the mirrors stood about three meters apart, the separation that matched the star's disk. Every size record since descends from that experiment.

STAR-Antares.beat: How big: the red heart of Scorpius
STAR-Antares.question: How does Antares measure up against the other giant stars of the sky?
STAR-Antares.why: The summer sky's size record belongs to the red heart of Scorpius, a supergiant whose cool color and fierce brightness, taken together, can only mean a vast body.
STAR-Antares.answer: Antares spans about 680 times the Sun's width, a close rival to Betelgeuse among the largest stars the naked eye can see. In the Sun's place its surface would reach beyond the orbit of Mars, and stars only swell like this in the last stretch of a heavy star's life, a short fuse that turns the stars of any crowd into a clock.
STAR-Antares.story: Antares lies close to the path of the Moon, which every so often passes in front of it, and those occultations make a natural ruler. A point-like star vanishes behind the Moon's edge almost instantly, but a star with a measurable disk fades over a fraction of a second, and the timing of that fade, recorded with fast detectors, gives its width on the sky. Combine the width with the distance and the true size follows, an old method that interferometers have since confirmed.

HD58061.beat: How big: the largest star in binocular reach
HD58061.question: Where is the largest star your binoculars can reach?
HD58061.why: Every size record so far has a bigger rival, and the chain ends here, at a faint orange point near τ Canis Majoris.
HD58061.answer: It is right here in Canis Major: VY Canis Majoris is about 1,420 times the Sun's width, nearly twice Betelgeuse, and in the Sun's place it would reach beyond Jupiter's orbit. Like every star this swollen it is heavy and near its end, for heavy stars live fast, and that rule turns the stars missing from a crowd into a measure of its age.
HD58061.story: Its size has swung widely as methods improved. Estimates of around two thousand times the Sun's width fell to a few hundred when one study found its surface warmer than assumed, and interferometer measurements later settled on a figure in between. A warmer surface shines more per square meter, so the same total light needs less surface, which means a size record leans on a temperature as much as on a distance.

HR472.beat: How hot: hot poles, cool waist
HR472.question: Is a star that spins this fast hotter at its poles than at its waist?
HR472.why: Achernar spins so close to its limit that its outline is stretched, and a stretched star cannot have one temperature, a hard test for the color thermometer.
HR472.answer: It is, because spin lifts its equator farther from the center, where gravity is weaker and the gas glows cooler, while the poles stay hot and bright. The temperature read from its color is an average over that lopsided surface, so turning it into a size needs a ruler laid in more than one direction.
HR472.story: Hugo von Zeipel predicted in 1924 that a spinning star should glow hotter at its poles than at its stretched waist, but seeing it needs a star wide enough on the sky to show both. Achernar, near, bright and flattened, is one of the few, and interferometers in Chile, combining telescopes many meters apart, traced how its brightness falls away from pole to equator.

HR3982.beat: How hot: a star with two temperatures
HR3982.question: Why does Regulus run hotter at its poles than at its waist?
HR3982.why: Regulus spins so fast that no single color describes it, which makes it the sharpest test of reading a temperature from starlight.
