HR3982.answer: Spin flings its equator outward, farther from the star's center, where gravity is weaker and the gas runs thousands of degrees cooler than at the poles. A spinning star's temperature is an average over a lopsided surface, so its size, which comes from dividing its power by that heat, depends on where you lay the ruler too.
HR3982.story: In 1924 Hugo von Zeipel worked out that a spinning star must glow hotter and brighter where its gravity is strongest, at the poles, and dimmer at its stretched equator. Interferometers at the CHARA array confirmed it for Regulus in 2005, measuring both its squashed outline and the heat falling away from pole to waist. We see Regulus from the side, so its cooler waist fills more of the view and the star looks cooler overall than its poles really are.

HR7557.beat: How hot: a star with two temperatures
HR7557.question: How can one star be two temperatures at once?
HR7557.why: Altair spins so fast that its surface has no single temperature, a puzzle for anyone trying to read heat from a star's color.
HR7557.answer: Its poles run hotter than its stretched equator, because gravity is weaker out at the waist and the gas there glows cooler and dimmer. The pictures of its surface that showed that difference also showed that a size can depend on where you lay the ruler, for Altair is wider across its waist than from pole to pole.
HR7557.story: Altair's disk is only about three thousandths of an arcsecond across, far too small for any single telescope. Interferometers get around that by combining light from telescopes hundreds of meters apart, which then see detail as fine as one giant mirror of that width would, and by moving the telescopes around they build up an image piece by piece. Altair, near and bright, was one of the first stars on which the trick produced an actual picture rather than a single size.

HR1325.beat: How big: the smallest star in reach
HR1325.question: What is the smallest star you can see with binoculars?
HR1325.why: Power and heat give size at the small end too, and the classic tiny star within binocular reach is the dead core that orbits 40 Eridani.
HR1325.answer: The smallest is 40 Eridani B, a white dwarf, the crushed core a star leaves after shedding its giant envelope, and its cooling clock says it became one only about 122 million years ago. Every white dwarf began as a star that ran out of fuel, and how soon that happens depends on its weight, which is why the dead and the swollen together tell the age of a crowd.
HR1325.story: Its smallness was confirmed by a test of Einstein's gravity. Light climbing out of a very compact star loses a little energy and is shifted toward the red, by an amount that depends on the star's mass divided by its radius, and in the 1950s Daniel Popper measured that shift in 40 Eridani B. With the mass known from the orbit, the shift gave a radius close to the Earth's, the same answer its faintness and heat had already implied.

NGC5139.beat: How old: the heaviest ball of stars
NGC5139.question: How heavy is the heaviest ball of stars in our galaxy?
NGC5139.why: The richest crowd the Milky Way owns is the fuzzy star in Centaurus that the eye alone can find, and every one of its millions of stars is ancient.
NGC5139.answer: Omega Centauri holds about 3.9 million Suns' worth of stars, more than four times the mass of 47 Tucanae, the runner-up in brightness. Every one of its heavy stars burned out billions of years ago, and among the survivors are pulsing stars that all shine with nearly the same true power, so finding their kind far away gives a distance.
NGC5139.story: A cluster is weighed by how fast its stars move. In a heavy crowd, stars must swarm faster to avoid falling inward, so the spread of their speeds, measured from Doppler shifts along our line of sight and from their drift across the sky, gives the total mass inside their orbits. Omega Centauri's random speeds are among the highest of any globular, and the mass they imply is a record none of the galaxy's other clusters matches.

NGC104.question: How old are the stars in the sky's second-brightest globular cluster?
NGC104.why: 47 Tucanae, second only to Omega Centauri in brightness, packs its ancient stars so tightly that its core looks almost like a single star.
NGC104.answer: 47 Tucanae is about 11.75 billion years old, an age read from the heaviest stars still burning core hydrogen, which are only now running out, since everything heavier burned out long before. Its brightest red giants have reached a limit every old star hits at nearly the same true power, and that shared ceiling, seen in a far galaxy, tells how far away it is.
NGC104.story: A crowd this rich is a place where stars meet. Near its packed center, stars pass close enough to swap partners, and dead stars captured into tight pairs are spun up by the matter they draw from their companions until they turn hundreds of times a second; radio telescopes have found dozens of these millisecond pulsars here. Such encounters are so rare in thin crowds that their number is itself a record of how densely the cluster is packed.

NGC7789.beat: How old: the heaviest nearby open cluster
NGC7789.question: Why has the heaviest open cluster near us survived for over a billion years?
NGC7789.why: Most star families dissolve within a few hundred million years, so the open clusters that last are record holders, and none within thousands of light-years is heavier than Caroline's Rose.
NGC7789.answer: Its own gravity is the reason, for nearly 18,000 Suns' worth of stars hold each other against the galactic tides that unravel lighter families. A census that complete also gives every kind of star in it a measured output, and stars of a known kind, found far beyond parallax, give their distances away.
NGC7789.story: No one can weigh every member of a cluster, so its mass is built up from a census. Gaia counts the members bright enough to measure, and the well-known proportion of small, faint stars to large, bright ones, roughly the same in every family, fills in the many too faint to see. The total is then checked against how tightly the members are held, and for this cluster both routes point to an unusually heavy family.

M11.beat: How rich: one of the richest open clusters
M11.question: How many stars crowd into the Wild Duck Cluster?
M11.why: The record for crowding among open clusters goes to a handful of families, and the Wild Duck, so rich it is often mistaken for a globular, is one of them.
M11.answer: Gaia counts about 1,900 members bright enough to detect, packed into a fan only about 30 light-years across, and the true number is larger still. Its heaviest stars have already begun to swell and die, which dates it to a few hundred million years, and so many kinds of star at one distance make it a reference for stars too far for parallax.
M11.story: Counting a cluster's members is harder than it sounds when it lies in front of the Scutum star cloud, one of the densest stretches of the Milky Way. Gaia does it by motion: true members drift across the sky together, at the same rate and in the same direction, while background stars wander every which way, so the cluster stands out in a plot of motions even where it is lost among the stars. The spread of those shared motions then shows how strongly the members are held, a weight read from their speeds.

M67.beat: How old: the oldest open cluster in Messier's list
M67.question: How old is the oldest open cluster in Messier's catalog?
M67.why: Among the open clusters in Messier's list, M67 has lost the most: every star much heavier than the Sun is already gone, and the family is still together.
M67.answer: M67 is about 3.9 billion years old, close to the Sun's own age, so its surviving stars are a family portrait of stars like ours. Stars of a known kind and a known age shine with a known power, and that is what lets the same kind of star, found much farther away, give away its own distance.
M67.story: This cluster owes its long life partly to its address. It sits well above the thin disk of the galaxy, out of the layer where giant gas clouds drift, and since passing clouds are what tear most clusters apart, a cluster that spends much of its time above them is spared most of the damage. Its orbit has kept it out of harm's way for billions of years, long enough for every heavy member to burn out while the family stayed together.

M92.beat: How old: among the oldest clusters known
M92.question: How old are the stars in one of the oldest clusters in the Milky Way?
M92.why: M92, a compact glow in Hercules often passed over for its famous neighbor, has been losing its heavy stars for longer than almost anything in the galaxy.
M92.answer: M92 comes out at about 13.8 billion years by one careful study and 12.75 by another, so the safe claim is among the very oldest anywhere. Old crowds like this one also hold pulsing stars whose true power is fixed by their kind, and those stars carry distances out to other galaxies.
M92.story: An age this great is a test for cosmology as well as for stars. The universe itself, timed from the faint afterglow of the Big Bang, comes out at about the same figure, so the oldest clusters must have formed within its first few hundred million years, or the models of stars or of the universe are wrong somewhere. So far the two clocks, one read from starlight and one from the early universe, leave just enough room for each other.

M30.beat: How old: among the oldest clusters dated
M30.question: How old is the small glow beside 41 Capricorni?
M30.why: Among 55 globular clusters dated in one large study, M30 came out among the oldest, so this small glow sits near the top of the age record.
M30.answer: M30 is about 13 billion years old, nearly three times the age of the Sun and Earth. Every star even a little heavier than the Sun has had time to live and die here, and the giants that remain all top out at nearly the same true brightness, a ceiling that serves as a ruler wherever old stars can be seen.
M30.story: Comparing clusters with one another is more precise than dating any one of them alone. If two clusters share the same chemistry, the difference between their turnoffs depends only on age, so a survey with a single camera and a single method can rank dozens of clusters even where the absolute ages remain uncertain. In such rankings the clusters poorest in heavy elements come out almost the same age, a hint that the galaxy built its first star cities in one early burst.

M13.beat: How old: the great Hercules cluster
M13.question: How old are the half million stars of the great Hercules cluster?
M13.why: The age records of northern skies are held by globular clusters, and the Great Hercules Cluster, the brightest of them in the far-northern sky, is the grand example.
M13.answer: The Great Hercules Cluster is about 12 billion years old, dated from the point where its stars are just now leaving their steady middle age. Old stars of a known kind shine with a predictable power, and spotting their kind in another galaxy is how that galaxy's distance can be read.
M13.story: In the 1990s globular clusters caused a crisis: their turnoffs implied ages of fifteen billion years or more, older than the universe was thought to be. Part of the fix came from Hipparcos, whose parallaxes of nearby old stars showed the clusters to be somewhat farther, and so their stars brighter, than assumed; brighter turnoff stars are heavier, and heavier stars mean a younger cluster. The cluster ages came down, the universe turned out older than thought, and the two now agree.

M22.beat: How old: the first globular cluster found
M22.question: How old is the first globular cluster anyone ever discovered?
M22.why: Abraham Ihle stumbled on this ball of stars in 1665, and it holds two records at once, the first globular ever found and one of the nearest and brightest.
M22.answer: The Sagittarius Cluster is nearly three times as old as the Sun, a figure read from the faintest stars still burning hydrogen. Its old giants and pulsing stars shine with a power the cluster's distance pins down, and stars of known power are exactly what it takes to measure much farther things.
M22.story: This cluster is a harder clock to read than its brightness suggests. It lies toward the crowded center of the galaxy behind a patchy veil of dust that dims some of its stars more than others, and its members may not all share one chemistry, since some studies find two groups with different amounts of heavy elements. Astronomers correct for the dust star by star before reading the turnoff, and the age that survives those corrections is what the record rests on.

NGC6397.beat: How old: a clock of dead stars
NGC6397.question: Why does being the second-nearest globular make this cluster such a good clock?
NGC6397.why: Nearness and age meet here, since NGC 6397 is the second-nearest globular cluster, close enough for its faintest dead stars to be seen and timed.
NGC6397.answer: Only in a cluster this close, about 8,100 light-years away, can the very faintest white dwarfs be found, the ones that have been cooling longest. They have been fading for about 11.5 billion years, and the same nearness that makes the clock readable also shows how bright old stars truly are, a ruler for crowds much farther away.
NGC6397.story: White dwarfs make a good clock because they are simple. With no fuel left, each one just radiates away the heat it was born with, at a rate physics can predict, and deep inside the oldest ones the carbon and oxygen slowly freeze into a crystal, releasing heat that briefly slows their fading. Models must include that delay, and Gaia has since seen its signature among nearby white dwarfs, which is why the cooling clock is trusted for clusters like this one.

M4.beat: How old: the nearest globular cluster
M4.question: How far is the nearest globular cluster, and how old are its stars?
M4.why: The age records belong to globular clusters, and the nearest one of all sits about a degree from Antares, a perfect place to measure one up close.
M4.answer: M4 lies about 6,000 light-years away, roughly ten times farther than Antares beside it, and its stars are about 11.5 billion years old, dated both from the stars now leaving middle age and from the coolest white dwarfs. Two clocks agreeing is what makes the age trustworthy, and stars this well measured show what old stars truly shine like, which is how much farther ones are ranged.
M4.story: Being the nearest does not make it easy to measure. It lies behind the dusty clouds around Antares, and that dust is unusual, dimming light more for the reddening it causes than ordinary dust does, so the standard correction would put the cluster at the wrong distance. Its pulsing stars, measured in infrared light where dust matters little, helped settle the figure, and with the distance firm the turnoff gives a trustworthy age.

M15.beat: How old: one of the most iron-poor globulars
M15.question: What does a star cluster's lack of iron say about its age?
M15.why: Iron is made in stars and scattered when they die, so a cluster with almost none is a record of how early it formed, and the Great Pegasus Globular is one of the poorest known.
M15.answer: It says the cluster formed early, and the dying of its stars agrees, putting it at about 12.75 billion years. Old, iron-poor stars like these shine with a predictable power, and a star of known power, seen faint, tells you how far away it is.
M15.story: A star's iron is counted from the strength of the iron lines in its spectrum: the fewer iron atoms in its atmosphere, the fainter those lines, and stars in this cluster show them so weakly that they barely register beside the Sun's. Because each generation of stars adds iron to the galaxy's gas, a low count is a calendar, though only a relative one: it says early, and the turnoff says how early.

HD140283.beat: How old: one of the oldest single stars
HD140283.question: How old is one of the oldest stars whose age is well measured?
HD140283.why: Age records usually belong to whole clusters, but this lone faint star in Libra rivals the oldest of them, a visitor from the galaxy's youth.
HD140283.answer: HD 140283 is about 12 billion years old, give or take half a billion, as old as the most ancient globular clusters and far older than any star around it. Its age hangs on its distance, and the reasoning can also run backward: once old stars of its kind have a known power, finding them far away gives a distance.
HD140283.story: Most lone stars cannot be dated well, but this one is caught at a revealing moment. It has just left its steady hydrogen-burning life and is crossing the brief subgiant stage, where a star's brightness depends sharply on how long it has lived, so a precise distance, and therefore a precise true brightness, translates almost directly into an age. That is why its age record rests on a parallax as much as on any model.

M37.beat: How old: the richest of Auriga's three
M37.question: Which of Auriga's three Messier clusters is the richest, and the oldest?
M37.why: Auriga holds three clusters in a short sweep, and M37 takes both local records, the most stars and the most years.
M37.answer: M37 wins both, and binoculars show the age as a grainy glow where its younger neighbors sparkle: its bright blue stars are long gone, leaving thousands of modest stars under a few orange giants. A family that large at one known distance is a full set of reference lamps, every kind with its true output measured, ready to be recognized where parallax cannot reach.
M37.story: Richness and age go together for a reason. A cluster loses members steadily to passing clouds and the galaxy's tides, and a poor one is gone within a few hundred million years, so only families born rich survive long enough to grow old. This cluster started with enough stars to outlast that erosion, which is why the oldest of Auriga's three is also the most populous.

M3.beat: How old: a crowd full of pulsing stars
M3.question: Why are M3's many pulsing stars a sign of its great age?
M3.why: M3 holds a record for the number of its stars caught in the act of pulsing, and those throbbing stars matter far beyond the cluster itself.
M3.answer: At least 274 of its stars are known to vary, most of them RR Lyrae stars. Each was born a little lighter than the Sun, has already been a giant and now burns helium, a stage that stars so light reach only in the oldest crowds. So their presence dates the cluster, and since stars of their kind all shine with nearly one true brightness, each of them is a ruler wherever it is found.
M3.story: Solon Bailey sorted this cluster's pulsers by the shapes of their light curves around 1900, and his classes are still in use. The stars throb because a layer of their outer gas acts like a valve, trapping heat as it is squeezed and letting it go as it expands, the same engine that drives the brighter Cepheids.

M31.beat: How far, run backward: the farthest naked-eye object
M31.question: How far away is the most distant thing most people can see unaided?
M31.why: Every rung so far turned a distance into something else, and the last one runs backward, using stars of known power to reach a distance no parallax could.
M31.answer: The Andromeda Galaxy lies about 2.5 million light-years away, so the light reaching you set out before our species existed. Its pulsing stars, whose power the lower rungs taught astronomers to read, look so faint that only a distance in the millions of light-years could explain them.
M31.story: The figure doubled once. In the early 1950s Walter Baade found that astronomers had been mixing two kinds of pulsing stars with different brightness rules, and that Andromeda's Cepheids were brighter than assumed; brighter stars that look equally faint must be farther away, so the galaxy's distance, along with the size of the known universe, roughly doubled. Today eclipsing pairs of stars in Andromeda give a geometric check that agrees with the Cepheids.

M33.beat: How far, run backward: the eye's farthest reach
M33.question: How far can the unaided eye reach on the very darkest night?
M33.why: Stars of known power, seen faint, give a distance, and Triangulum, Andromeda's smaller neighbor, is the farthest place the unaided eye can follow that rule.
M33.answer: The Triangulum Galaxy lies about 2.7 million light-years away, a little beyond Andromeda, a distance measured from 154 Cepheids timed by Hubble. Only an exceptionally dark site lets the eye pick it up, so the farthest record you can claim depends as much on your sky as on the galaxy.
M33.story: Triangulum has also been ranged without any pulsing stars. Radio telescopes linked across continents followed clouds of water vapor glowing like natural lasers in two of its star-forming regions, and as the galaxy turned, their drift across the sky could be compared with their speeds from the Doppler effect. The two match at only one distance, and it lands close to the Cepheid figure, the kind of agreement that makes a distance record trustworthy.

LMC.beat: How far, run backward: the anchor galaxy
LMC.question: How far away is the galaxy that anchors the whole cosmic distance ladder?
LMC.why: A star of known power, seen faint, gives a distance, and every such ruler beyond our galaxy is anchored on one well-measured neighbor, the Large Magellanic Cloud.
LMC.answer: The Large Magellanic Cloud lies about 162,000 light-years away, roughly ten times as far as the bright globular clusters around our galaxy, yet binoculars still pick out its clusters and the Tarantula Nebula. Those knots are star cities of another galaxy, and the Tarantula is the brightest star-forming region in our whole galactic neighborhood.
LMC.story: The Cloud's distance has also been measured with a single exploding star. When the supernova of 1987 lit up a ring of gas around it, the ring did not brighten all at once: light reached its near side first and its far side later, and the delay gave the ring's true size in light-days. Comparing that with the ring's size in Hubble's images gave a distance, a geometric check on the anchor of the cosmic ladder.

SMC.beat: How far, run backward: where the rule was found
SMC.question: Where did astronomers learn to measure the farthest distances of all?
SMC.why: The ladder's last step needs stars whose power can be read from afar, and the rule that made that possible was found in this faint cloud of stars in 1912.
SMC.answer: In the Small Magellanic Cloud, about 204,000 light-years away, where Henrietta Leavitt found that a Cepheid's rhythm gives away its power. With that rule, the faintness of a pulsing star became a measure of its distance, and the distance record could finally leave the Milky Way.
SMC.story: Leavitt's rule told how much brighter one Cepheid was than another, but not how bright any of them truly was, so the Cloud's distance was still unknown. Within a year Ejnar Hertzsprung calibrated it with Cepheids in our own galaxy, and his first figure came out far too small, partly from a slip and partly from dust no one yet allowed for. The rule was right from the start; it took decades of better calibration to make the ruler read true.

NGC5128.beat: How far, run backward: a giant elliptical
NGC5128.question: How far away is the faint glow just north of Omega Centauri?
NGC5128.why: From a star city of our own galaxy to a whole giant galaxy is one binocular hop, and Centaurus A is ranged the backward way, from dying stars whose true brightness is known.
NGC5128.answer: Centaurus A lies about 700 times farther than Omega Centauri, which looks so much brighter beside it, so the faint smudge must be a giant indeed, the nearest giant elliptical galaxy in the sky. The two glows in one sweep span the whole ladder, from a cluster inside our galaxy to a galaxy far beyond our own group.
NGC5128.story: One of the ways to range a galaxy of old stars uses their dying shells. In any large galaxy the brightest planetary nebulae, glowing in the green light of oxygen, top out at nearly the same true brightness, so finding the bright end of their numbers gives a distance, and for Centaurus A it agrees with the other methods. A galaxy with no pulsing stars of the usual kind can still be measured, as long as its stars keep dying in a recognizable way.

M81.beat: How far, run backward: beyond our own group
M81.question: How far beyond Andromeda can binoculars reach to find a whole galaxy?
M81.why: Andromeda belongs to our own small group of galaxies, and Bode's Galaxy, one of the brightest beyond it, is ranged by stars whose power is already known.
M81.answer: Bode's Galaxy lies about 11.8 million light-years away, nearly five times as far as Andromeda, and it still shows as a clear oval with a starlike core. Its light set out about 12 million years ago, so the farthest record here is also the oldest light your eyes will catch tonight.
M81.story: The supernova that flared in this galaxy in the early 1990s gave a distance of its own. Radio telescopes linked across the Earth watched its expanding shell grow month by month, while spectra gave the speed of the expanding gas, and a speed matched to a growth on the sky fixes the distance. It broadly agrees with the Cepheids and the red giants, three independent rungs landing close to one number.

NGC253.beat: How far, run backward: a starburst galaxy
NGC253.question: How far away is the silvery streak low in Sculptor?
NGC253.why: The top rung of the ladder in this part of the sky lies beyond our own group of galaxies, in an edge-on spiral ranged by stars of known power seen very faint.
NGC253.answer: The Sculptor Galaxy lies about 11.4 million light-years away, more than four times the distance of Andromeda, so the light in your binoculars left it long before the first humans. It shows so well because it is a big spiral, and its core is also making stars at a furious rate.
NGC253.story: The Sculptor Galaxy belongs to one of the nearest groups of galaxies beyond our own, a loose gathering strung out along our line of sight. It also lies almost exactly toward the south pole of the Milky Way, where little of our galaxy's dust is in the way, so its light reaches us with hardly any dimming to correct for. That clean view makes its distance one of the steadier ones at this range.

M83.beat: How far, run backward: the Southern Pinwheel
M83.question: How far away is the first galaxy ever found beyond our own group?
M83.why: Found in 1752, long before anyone knew what galaxies were, this face-on spiral turned out to lie far beyond Andromeda, once stars of known power could be picked out in it.
M83.answer: The Southern Pinwheel lies about 16 million light-years away, more than six times as far as Andromeda, a distance measured with its brightest red giants and its Cepheids. Its discoverer saw only a faint round glow, and it took the whole ladder of records, from parallax to pulsing stars, to put a number on it.
M83.story: Galaxies gather in groups held by their mutual gravity, and ours, the Local Group, is dominated by the Milky Way and Andromeda. The Southern Pinwheel belongs to a different gathering, the group around Centaurus A, whose members share a distance and move together through space. Recognizing that a galaxy lies in another group needs its distance first, which is why the maps of nearby groups came only after the ladder reached this far.

M49.beat: How far, run backward: into the Virgo Cluster
M49.question: How far does the light of this faint round glow in Virgo travel?
M49.why: The distance record ends in a crowd of galaxies, the Virgo Cluster, and M49, the first of its members ever found, was ranged by rulers each calibrated on the rung below.
M49.answer: M49 lies about 55 million light-years away, more than twenty times as far as Andromeda, and it still shows as a small round glow because it is a giant, one of the largest galaxies in the Virgo Cluster. Few things binoculars can show lie farther.
M49.story: Galaxies this far are ranged by rungs that each lean on the one below. The Hubble Space Telescope found Cepheids in spiral galaxies of the Virgo Cluster in the 1990s, and those calibrated the smoother methods that work for giant ellipticals like this one, whose old stars do not pulse. The whole cluster lies at roughly one distance, so a ruler checked on one member serves for the rest.

M54.beat: How far, run backward: a cluster from another galaxy
M54.question: How far away is the faint smudge near the bottom of the Teapot?
M54.why: On summer nights the distance record needs no bright galaxy, for this small globular belongs to another galaxy, ranged by old stars whose true power is known.
M54.answer: M54 lies about 86,000 light-years away, so its light passes beneath the galaxy's crowded central bulge on its way to you, and it is visible at all only because it is enormous. The galaxy it belongs to is being torn apart by our own, so tonight's farthest record is a cluster caught in the act of changing galaxies.
M54.story: This cluster's membership in another galaxy rests on its motion. Its stars recede from us at about the same speed as the stars of the faint dwarf galaxy around it, far faster than the Milky Way's own stars in that direction, and it lies at the same distance, deep behind our galaxy's center. A cluster that matches a galaxy in both distance and speed belongs to it, which is how a summer globular turned out to be a visitor.

M53.beat: How far, run backward: the galaxy's outskirts
M53.question: How far out in the galaxy's halo does this small glow in Coma lie?
M53.why: Not every distance record needs another galaxy: M53 orbits in the outer halo of our own, so far out that only old stars of known power can range it.
M53.answer: M53 lies about 60,000 light-years out, roughly two and a half times as far as the Great Hercules Cluster, so even its half a million Suns' worth of stars shrink to a small haze. The spring sky looks out of the Milky Way's disk here, and M53 marks how far our galaxy's outskirts reach into that darkness.
M53.story: Clusters like this one first showed astronomers where the center of the galaxy is. In 1918 Harlow Shapley measured the distances of dozens of globulars and found them gathered around a point far off in Sagittarius rather than around the Sun, and he reasoned that they swarm around the galaxy's true center. This cluster, far above the plane of the galaxy, is one of the outlying ones that showed how far the swarm extends.

M94.beat: How far, run backward: a galaxy beyond our group
M94.question: How far away is the fuzzy star three degrees north of Cor Caroli?
M94.why: In the spring sky the distance record leaves our galaxy altogether, and M94 is ranged the backward way, by stars of known power seen very faint.
M94.answer: M94 lies about 15 million light-years away, roughly six times as far as Andromeda, so the faint fuzzy star in your binoculars is a whole spiral galaxy seen across that gulf. It shows at all because so much of its light is gathered into a small, bright center.
M94.story: Its distance comes from its old red giants. A red giant brightens as it ages until its core grows hot enough to ignite helium, and that ignition happens at nearly the same core mass in every old star, so the brightest red giants in any galaxy top out at one true brightness. Hubble picked out where this galaxy's red giants stop climbing, and how faint that ceiling looks gives the distance.

NGC3532.beat: How rich: the Wishing Well Cluster
NGC3532.question: How rich is the Wishing Well Cluster, and why is it still a cluster at all?
NGC3532.why: Three degrees from the Carina Nebula lies one of the richest open clusters known, and its record is less about any single star than about how many have stayed together.
NGC3532.answer: Gaia counts about 3,400 members, some 4,900 Suns' worth of stars, and that sheer weight has kept the family recognizable for about 300 million years, long after a lighter cluster would have dissolved. Its heavy blue stars are already gone, which is how that age is read, and the survivors, all at one known distance, show what each kind of star truly shines like.
NGC3532.story: Every cluster has a boundary set by a tug of war: inside it the family's own gravity wins, and outside it the galaxy's tides take over and pull stragglers away. The heavier the cluster, the wider that boundary, so a rich family can keep members that have wandered far from its center. Astronomers find the boundary by counting how the density of members falls off with distance from the middle and where it stops falling.

HR4763.beat: How big: one of the widest-looking stars
HR4763.question: Why does Gacrux show one of the widest star disks in the whole sky?
HR4763.why: Gacrux, the orange star at the top of the Southern Cross, adds a twist to the size record: how big a star looks depends on its distance as well as its body.
HR4763.look: Gacrux is the head of the Cross, the one star of the five with a clear orange tint. Its disk is under a thirtieth of an arcsecond across, far too small for any binoculars, so what you see is a point, and the record has to be read from its light.
HR4763.answer: Gacrux is the nearest of the cool red giants, and that rare pairing of a swollen body with a short distance makes it look wider from here than almost any other star in the sky. Like every giant it is a star in its later years, swollen once its core ran out of hydrogen, and when that happens depends on its weight, which is how the giants of a crowd help date it.
HR4763.story: Even the widest-looking stars are points to a single telescope, so astronomers measure them by combining telescopes many meters apart, or by timing how quickly a star winks out when the Moon passes in front of it. Gacrux lies too far south for the Moon ever to cover it, so its width rests on its brightness and its temperature, which together fix how much glowing surface it must have.

HR1612.beat: How big: a giant with a passing partner
HR1612.question: How wide is the orange giant that hides its partner in the Kids?
HR1612.why: Sizes usually come from power and heat, but ζ Aurigae, in the little triangle of the Kids beside Capella, offers a second ruler in its eclipses.
HR1612.answer: The giant spans about 130 times the Sun's width, and the eclipses check that figure directly: the small star's known speed, multiplied by the time it stays hidden, gives the width of whatever hides it. Like every giant this size it is a heavy star in its later years, and because heavy stars reach that stage first, the giants a crowd still holds help date it.
HR1612.story: An eclipse measures a star in kilometers rather than in angles on the sky, so it needs no distance at all, a welcome check on sizes built from power and heat. ζ Aurigae gave its name to a small family of such pairs, among them VV Cephei and 31 Cygni, that astronomers use to test how far a supergiant's thin outer layers really reach.

HR1790.beat: How much light: Orion's nearer shoulder
HR1790.question: Do Orion's two shoulders, so alike in brightness, make the same amount of light?
HR1790.why: Bellatrix and Betelgeuse look nearly equal in brightness, and only their distances can say which one is working harder.
HR1790.answer: They do not, for Bellatrix pours out about 7,000 times the Sun's light, while Betelgeuse, about twice as far, must make many times more to look as bright. Two stars can match in looks and differ widely in power, and whether that power comes from heat or from size is written in their colors, blue-white for one and orange for the other.
HR1790.story: Comparing two stars' power takes more than their distances. Betelgeuse sends much of its light out as infrared and Bellatrix much of its as ultraviolet, both invisible, so each visible glow has to be scaled up before the totals can be compared, and the corrections run in opposite directions.

HR2693.beat: How big: the Great Dog's yellow supergiant
HR2693.question: How big must Wezen be, with a surface barely hotter than the Sun's?
HR2693.why: Wezen, the creamy star of the Great Dog's hindquarters, has a surface close to the Sun's in heat, so its great power has to come from somewhere else.
HR2693.answer: Each square meter of Wezen shines only a little more than the Sun's, so its 37,000 Suns' worth of light has to pour from a vast surface, and the arithmetic gives a body roughly 190 times the Sun's width. Like every swollen supergiant it is a heavy star late in life, and because heavy stars reach that stage first, giants like it are a clock for any crowd that holds them.
HR2693.story: Yellow supergiants are caught in passage. A heavy star swelling from a hot blue youth toward a cool red old age crosses this band of temperatures quickly, so few stars are seen in it at any moment, which is why most of the sky's largest stars are red and a yellow one this bright is worth a long look.

HR2773.beat: How big: the orange supergiant of Puppis
HR2773.question: How large is the deep orange star that glows beside Naos?
HR2773.why: Pi Puppis glows deep orange about ten degrees from Naos, a cool star beside a hot one, and that coolness is what turns its power into a size.
HR2773.answer: Put in the Sun's place, its surface would reach a little past the orbit of the Earth, which is what a surface that cool needs to give out as much light as it does. Because heavier stars reach this swollen stage sooner, which stars a crowd has swollen or lost is a measure of its age.
HR2773.story: When a heavy star's core runs out of hydrogen, the core shrinks and heats while the layers above it do the opposite, swelling and cooling, as if the star were turning itself inside out. The energy still has to escape, so the surface grows until enough cool square meters can carry it, and the star turns from blue-white to orange in a brief chapter of its life.

HR7796.beat: How much light: the heart of the Northern Cross
HR7796.question: How much light does Sadr, at the heart of the Northern Cross, really make?
HR7796.why: Sadr looks like an ordinary second-magnitude star, and only its distance, read against its brightness, shows what it really is.
HR7796.look: Sadr is the star where the long and short bars of the Northern Cross meet, a pale yellowish point in a field crowded with fainter Milky Way stars. Its tint is close to the Sun's, which makes what it is doing all the more surprising.
HR7796.answer: Sadr pours out roughly 34,000 times the Sun's light, a figure its faintness hides until the distance is known. Power on that scale might come from heat or from size, and Sadr's yellowish tint, close to the Sun's own, already hints which.
HR7796.story: Turning a glow into a power takes two corrections besides the distance. Dust in the crowded plane of the galaxy dims and reddens Sadr's light on its way to you, so some of the loss has to be added back, and the light the eye cannot see, ultraviolet and infrared, has to be counted too. For a yellow star like Sadr the second correction is small, since its light peaks close to where our eyes are most sensitive.

HR8262.beat: How cold: a pulsing red giant
HR8262.question: How cool is the reddish star pulsing beside ρ Cygni?
HR8262.why: A cool surface is where color says the most, and W Cygni, a red giant about ten degrees east of Deneb, wears its temperature openly.
HR8262.look: Center ρ Cygni, about ten degrees east of Deneb, and W Cygni is the reddish star just to its south-east. Set its orange-red against yellowish ρ Cygni beside it, and the color gap you see is a temperature gap.
HR8262.answer: Its surface runs at about 3,400 K, a little over half the Sun's temperature, so each square meter of it gives out only about a tenth of the Sun's light. A star that cool still shining in binoculars from about 630 light-years must be spread over a vast surface, and its power and heat together say how vast.
HR8262.story: A star like this does not hold one temperature for long. As W Cygni swells and shrinks, its surface warms and cools with it, and in the cooler phases the bands of molecules in its spectrum deepen and dim its visible light. A single temperature quoted for it is an average over the cycle, read from how deep those bands run.

M35.beat: How old: the cluster at Gemini's feet
M35.question: How old is M35, and do two different clocks agree on it?
M35.why: M35, at Gemini's feet, is young enough that its age has been read two ways, from the stars it has lost and from how fast its Sun-like stars still spin.
M35.answer: Both clocks agree that it is a young crowd, a little older than the Pleiades: its heaviest blue stars are already gone, and its Sun-like stars have only begun to brake. With M35's stars at one known distance, each kind has a measured output, and the same kinds looking much fainter in NGC 2158 are one way that cluster's distance is read.
M35.story: The faint patch beside it, NGC 2158, looks like a junior companion but lies several times farther away and is roughly ten times older. Side by side they show the age rule at work: M35 still holds hot blue-white stars, while its old neighbor's brightest members have long since turned yellow and orange.

M39.beat: How old: a loose crowd near Deneb
M39.question: How long can a small, loose crowd like M39 hold together?
M39.why: M39, a short sweep from Deneb, is a light and loosely held family, a useful contrast to the rich crowds that last for billions of years.
M39.answer: M39 has already held together for a few hundred million years, but a family this light is being pulled apart by the galaxy's tides and will probably scatter long before the rich crowds grow old. Until it does, its roughly five hundred members, all at one measured distance, are a ready-made sample of what each kind of star gives out.
M39.story: A cluster keeps only the members its own gravity can hold against the galaxy's pull, and that tug of war sets an edge around it. Each close passage between two members flings one of them a little faster, and stars nudged past the edge drift off in long trails, which Gaia has traced around the Hyades and the Beehive. The lighter the cluster, the nearer its edge and the faster it leaks.

M44.question: Is the Beehive the same age as the Hyades, and how could anyone tell?
M44.why: The Beehive is one of the nearest and brightest crowds in the sky, close enough that binoculars show the very stars its age is read from.
M44.answer: It very nearly is, for in both families the stars now swelling into orange giants have the same weight, and stars of one weight take the same time to reach that stage. With its distance pinned down, the Beehive also gives each of its kinds of star a true output, a standard that any farther cluster holding the same kinds can be measured against.
M44.story: Nearly every age record is read from a chart of color against brightness. A cluster's stars lie along one band until, at a certain brightness, the band bends off toward the giants, and that bend marks the heaviest stars still burning hydrogen in their cores. The older the cluster, the fainter and redder the bend, and for the Beehive it falls among white stars two to three times as heavy as the Sun.

M93.beat: How old: the arrowhead of Puppis
M93.question: How long ago did M93 lose its blue stars?
M93.why: M93 is a compact arrowhead of stars in Puppis, old enough that its brightest members are no longer the blue-white stars a young family shows.
M93.answer: Its family is about 740 million years old, long enough for every star much heavier than two Suns to burn out. With both its age and its distance measured, its survivors serve as reference stars, each kind with a known output, for families too far away for parallax.
M93.story: A heavier star carries more fuel but burns it so much faster that it dies far sooner, so in a family born together the stars drop out from the top down, heaviest first. As the family ages the top of its range keeps sinking, from blue giants to white stars and on toward stars like the Sun, and wherever the top stands now is the reading on its clock.
